**Sūrat al-Mujādila** (The Pleading Woman)

Its purpose is to inform of the severe punishment, which the Iron (sūrah) alluded to, that befalls those who oppose Allah and His Messenger ﷺ. This follows from His perfect knowledge, which entails perfect power, which in turn entails encompassing all the attributes of perfection. This is indicated by its name, al-Mujādila, given on account of the beginning and the end of its story, and by the repetition of the Greatest Name, which is comprehensive, throughout the story and the whole surah, a repetition not found in any other surah, such that no verse is free of it. As for the verses in which each of the two names recurs twice or more, the multiplicity of each of these serves to show that most of those addressed in them are people who may be regarded at one time with majesty and at another with perfection, so both descriptions are joined for them. These are people who have believed but have committed a lapse or a disobedience. For this reason the surah includes matters in which He sternly rebuked some of the people of faith when they fell into them, and did not permit them to do so, returning the law to what the natural inclination calls for, as He did in other matters, such as eating and intercourse during the nights of Ramadan without distinguishing between wakefulness and sleep, because these contradict wisdom and are far from the requirements of mercy. [p. 332] This confirms what preceded concerning the secret of the omission of al-Wāqi'a, al-Raḥmān and al-Qamar from this comprehensive name. And Allah is the Granter of success.

**"In the name of Allah"** Whose knowledge encompasses all things, so that His power is complete and all His attributes are perfected, **"the Most Gracious"** Who has embraced all creation with the generosity of bringing them into existence and sending their guides, **"the Most Merciful"** Who has singled out His chosen ones, so that His favour through His good pleasure is complete upon them.

* *

When al-Ḥadīd was concluded, after establishing the inability of creation and the great favour of Allah, the Exalted, and since hearing the voices of all creatures without one voice distracting from another or one speech from another is among the great bounties, and since the innovation of some worshippers in monasticism (rahbāniyya) had preceded, in matters for which no explicit permission had been given, which became a cause of wasting (themselves), and since ẓihār (the pre-Islamic formula of divorce by declaring one's wife unlawful to oneself by likening her to one's mother's back) was of two kinds, the time-bound and the absolute, and the time-bound kind was among what enters monasticism because it is a form of celibacy and the prohibition of what Allah has made lawful of the good things, and since some of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them all, had restrained themselves by means of the time-bound form from something desirable that had not come from Allah, and so made ẓihār from his wife out of scrupulousness in full devotion, fearing intercourse during the day of Ramadan, and since that was among what had not been permitted but was actually forbidden, as Abū Dāwūd related from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, and al-Ṭabarānī in al-Awsaṭ from Sahl ibn Ḥunayf, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Do not be severe upon yourselves, for those before you perished through their severity upon themselves, and you will find their remnants in the monasteries and the hermitages."

And some of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them all, had made absolute ẓihār, so his wife complained to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ of the harm that had befallen her and cried out to Allah. Allah's knowledge of the particulars of this poor woman's complaint and of the removal of her harm [by a ruling] general to her and to His other servants, such that her case became a general dispensation for the Muslims until the Day of Resurrection, informed that He is the Lord of great bounty, that He is the Manifest and the Hidden, and that the dominion is all His. He had commanded belief in Him and in His Messenger and promised light in return for it. The hearer of this was thus worthy of anticipating the clarification, which is the light, concerning this monasticism that had been innovated in this community, and of the lightening of the severity that had befallen some of them, so that the People of the Book might know what this community has of honour with its Lord, and that He singles out with His mercy whom He wills. So He said: **"Allah has indeed heard"** that is, He responded by His great bounty, which encompasses all the attributes of perfection, so His hearing embraced the voices **"the speech"** and He expressed it by a description rather than a name, to make known His all-embracing mercy, **"of her who pleads with you"** that is, who earnestly seeks to make you turn to her purpose **"concerning her husband"** that is, concerning the matter that frees him from his ẓihār, out of mercy to her **"and complains"** that is, she intentionally makes this pleading into a complaint, **"to Allah"** that is, the Sovereign, the Great, the Merciful, Who encompasses all things in knowledge. Because of her truthfulness in her complaint, and because she had cut off her hope of removing what afflicted her from anyone other than Allah, she and the Prophet ﷺ were both expecting that Allah would remove her harm. **"And Allah"** that is, while the One whose mercy embraces all things, because to Him belongs all command **"hears your dialogue"** that is, your mutual exchange, in which the answer of each of you returns to the other, as if, because of the weight of what had afflicted her matter and descended upon her harm, it arose from bewilderment.

Since this was at the utmost extreme of breaking custom, to the point that the truthful one, ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her, said when the verse was revealed: "Praise be to Allah, Who has embraced all voices with His hearing! She spoke to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ while I was at the side of the house, and I did not hear much of what she was saying," He emphasized it to draw attention to its great strangeness, and because those whose ignorance is great, due to their deep attachment to customs, might consider it unlikely. So He said: **"Indeed Allah"** that is, the One who encompasses all the attributes of perfection, so there is no equal to Him **"is All-Hearing, All-Seeing"** that is, of far-reaching hearing for everything heard, of sight for everything seen, and of knowledge for everything that may be known, from eternity to eternity. A similar correspondence has passed [p. 335] in al-Mā'ida, when He, the Exalted, followed the verse about the priests and monks with His saying, the Exalted: **"O you who believe, do not forbid the good things that Allah has made lawful for you"** [al-Mā'ida: 87]. However, this is particular and that is general, and this is one instance of it, so the correspondence is one, since the more specific is contained within the more general. The summary is that He, glorified be He, bestowed favour upon them by what He placed in their hearts of monasticism and other things, and informed that they did not fulfil its due, and that He gave their believers their reward, and commanded the Muslims to fear Allah and follow the Messenger ﷺ, so that they might obtain from His great bounty double what the People of the Book obtained, and forbade them from severity upon themselves through monasticism, so they became preferred in two respects: abundance of reward and lightness of works. **"That is the bounty of Allah, which He gives to whom He wills"** and Allah knows best. Al-Bazzār related from the route of Khaṣīf, from ʿAṭāʾ and from others also, from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, that "a man said: O Messenger of Allah! I made ẓihār from my wife, and I saw her leg in the moonlight, and I had intercourse with her before I expiated. He said: Expiate and do not repeat."

Abū Dāwūd related from ʿIkrima that "a man made ẓihār from his wife, then had intercourse with her before he expiated. He came to the Prophet ﷺ and informed him. He said: 'What led you to what you did?' He said: 'I saw the whiteness of her two legs in the moonlight.' He said: 'Keep away from her until you have expiated.'"

Al-Mundhirī said: He also related it from ʿIkrima from the Prophet ﷺ, and from ʿIkrima from [Ibn] ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, from the Prophet ﷺ, with the same meaning. [p. 336] It was also related by al-Nasā'ī, Ibn Māja and al-Tirmidhī, who said: [a] ḥasan gharīb ṣaḥīḥ [ḥadīth]. Al-Nasā'ī said: The mursal (version) is more correct than the musnad. Abū Bakr al-Mu'āfirī said: There is no sound ḥadīth on ẓihār on which one may rely. Al-Mundhirī said: There is room to dispute what he said, for al-Tirmidhī has authenticated it, as you see, its narrators are trustworthy, the hearing of some of them from others is well known, and ʿIkrima's narration from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, is one that al-Bukhārī relied upon in more than one place. End. And from al-Tirmidhī, who said it is ḥasan gharīb, from Salama ibn Ṣakhr, may Allah be pleased with him, concerning one who made ẓihār and had intercourse before expiating, he said: "One expiation only."

Al-Bayhaqi and al-Hakim also narrated it, through Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Thawban and Abu Salama ibn Abd al-Rahman, that Salama ibn Sakhr al-Bayadi (may Allah be pleased with him) made his wife unlawful to himself "like the back of his mother" (ẓihār), meaning that if he had intercourse with her until Ramadan ended. He mentioned this to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "Free a slave."

The story of Salama is the origin of the time-limited ẓihār (ẓihār, the pre-Islamic formula of divorce by comparing one's wife to one's mother). It shows that there is no return (ʿawd) in it, so no expiation (kaffārah) is owed for it except by intercourse with her during the period of ẓihār.

Abu Dawud narrated from Khuwayla bint Malik ibn Thaʿlaba (may Allah be pleased with her) that she said: "My husband Aws ibn al-Samit (may Allah be pleased with him) made ẓihār against me, so I came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) complaining to him, while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was disputing with me about it and saying: 'Fear Allah, for he is your paternal cousin.' I did not leave until the Qur'an was revealed: ﴿Allah has indeed heard﴾ up to the obligation. He said: 'Let him free a slave.' She said: 'He does not find one.' He said: 'Let him fast two consecutive months.' She said: 'O Messenger of Allah, he is an old man who has no strength for fasting.' He said: 'Then let him feed sixty needy persons.' She said: 'He has nothing to give in charity.' She said: 'Then at that moment a basket of dates was brought.' I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I will help him with another basket.' He said: 'You have done well. Go and feed sixty needy persons with it on his behalf, and return to your cousin.'" He said: "The ʿaraq is sixty ṣāʿ." In another report: "The ʿaraq is a basket that holds thirty ṣāʿ."

Al-Daraqutni narrated that Anas ibn Malik (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Aws ibn al-Samit (may Allah be pleased with him) made ẓihār against his wife Khuwayla bint Thaʿlaba (may Allah be pleased with her), and she complained to the Prophet (ﷺ), saying: 'He made ẓihār against me when my age grew old and my bones grew weak.' So Allah revealed the verse of ẓihār. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Aws: 'Free a slave.' He said: 'I have no means for that.' He said: 'Then fast two consecutive months.' He said: 'If I miss eating twice a day, my sight grows dim.' He said: 'Then feed sixty needy persons.' He said: 'I find nothing except that you help me with some of your provision and gift.' So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) helped him with fifteen ṣāʿ until Allah made it complete for him, and Allah is Merciful." He said: "They used to think that he had the same amount with him, and that was for sixty needy persons."

Also al-Daraqutni and al-Bayhaqi narrated that Khawla bint Thaʿlaba (may Allah be pleased with her) was seen by her husband, Aws ibn al-Samit, the brother of ʿUbada (may Allah be pleased with both of them), while she was praying. He solicited her, but she refused, so he became angry. He had some madness and levity in him, so he made ẓihār against her. She came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "Aws married me when I was young and desirable. When my age passed and I had lost my youth, he made me unlawful to himself like his mother."

Al-Tabarani narrated through Abu Maʿshar, from Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazi, who said: "Khawla bint Thaʿlaba was married to Aws ibn al-Samit, and he had some madness. In one of his fits of anger he said: 'You are unlawful to me like the back of my mother.' He said: 'I think you have become unlawful to me.' So she came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, Aws ibn al-Samit is the father of my children and the dearest of people to me. By the One who revealed the Book to you, he did not mention divorce.' He said: 'I do not see you except as having become unlawful to him.' She said: 'O Messenger of Allah, do not say that. By Allah, he did not mention divorce.' She kept arguing with the Prophet (ﷺ) many times, then she said: 'O Allah, I complain to You of my poverty and loneliness and what is hard for me of his separation.'" The hadith continues. And through Abu al-ʿAliya, who said: "Whenever he said to her, 'You have become unlawful to him,' she cried out and said: 'I complain to Allah,' and she did not move from her place until the verse was revealed."

Abu Dawud narrated from Hisham ibn ʿUrwa that Jamila was married to Aws ibn al-Samit, and he was a man with some madness. Whenever his madness intensified, he made ẓihār against his wife, so Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, revealed for him the expiation of ẓihār. He also narrated the same from the hadith of ʿUrwa, from ʿAʾisha (may Allah be pleased with her).

Al-Qushayri said: "In the report: she said, 'O Messenger of Allah! Aws married me when I was young, wealthy, with a family and much wealth. When my age grew old with him, my wealth was lost and my family scattered, he made me to him like the back of his mother. He has regretted and I have regretted. I have young children. If I take them to him they will be lost, and if I take them to myself they will go hungry.'" He meant that Allah then relieved her.

From this arises a question: many matters are judged by apparent knowledge, and then necessity changes that judgment for the one it affects. Al-Baghawi said: "This was the first ẓihār in Islam." Abu Hayyan said: "ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) used to honor Khawla (may Allah be pleased with her) whenever she entered upon him, and he would say: 'Allah has heard her.'" So the ẓihār in the hadith of Salama (may Allah be pleased with him) was time-limited, while in the hadith of Khawla (may Allah be pleased with her) it was unrestricted, and it was in the case of Salama. Whoever goes along with it is a monastic innovation (rahbāniyyah mubtadaʿah, a self-invented asceticism, a term used for the monasticism of the Christians) that did not observe its proper due, just as the monasticism of the Christians did not. The Prophet (ﷺ) did not follow it in its innovation as it should have been followed. As for the case of Khawla (may Allah be pleased with her), it was a calamity in which submission and not grieving should have been observed, as in the verse ﴿so that you may not despair﴾ [al-Hadid: 23]. Moreover, her refusal of her husband when he solicited her involved some inclination toward monasticism. Removing her complaint, although she was a weak woman, is of great virtue. What adds to its greatness is that He made it a general ruling for everyone in the entire Ummah who falls into it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (*Nazm al-Durar*) on surah 58, verse 2:

When God finished His report about the all-encompassing nature of His knowledge, He began again to report the ruling concerning the matter about which the woman was disputing (with the Prophet ﷺ). He said, condemning *ẓihār* (the pre-Islamic practice of likening one's wife to one's mother, a form of divorce) and clothing it in the garment of shame: ﴿Those who⁠﴾. Since *ẓihār* is reprehensible because it is a lie, He expressed it with the verbal form *tafaʿʿala* (تَفَعُّلِ), which indicates this, and said: ﴿[who] zihar⁠﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 33], meaning: they bring *ẓihār* into existence at any time [whenever it is] in Ramadan. It seems that He assimilated the *tāʾ* of *tafaʿʿala* and *mufāʿala* (the two verbal forms), because its reality is that the man removes what God has made lawful for him, namely intercourse with his wife.

Since *ẓihār* was specific to the Arabs and not shared by the other nations, He drew attention to this, as a way of disparaging it to them and condemning their custom regarding it, indicating that what was fitting for them was to be the furthest of people from this speech, because lying had always been considered repugnant among them in the *Jāhiliyyah* (the pre-Islamic period). Then Islam only increased its repugnance. So He said: ﴿from among you⁠﴾, meaning: O Arabs, the Muslims, who find lying repugnant in a way that others do not find it repugnant, and likewise whoever follows their religion, ﴿from their wives⁠﴾, meaning: they forbid their wives to themselves, by the prohibition of God upon them, the backs of their mothers, by one of them saying to his wife something from its explicit forms, such as: "You are to me like the back of my mother," or from its allusive forms, such as: "You are my mother." Every husband whose divorce is valid, his *ẓihār* is valid, whether he is free or a slave, a Muslim or a *dhimmī* (a protected non-Muslim), whether he has consummated the marriage or not, whether he is able to have intercourse or unable, whether the wife is young or old, sane or insane, whole or *ratqāʾ* (having an obstruction preventing intercourse), Muslim or *dhimmiyyah*, and even if she is revocable (in a *rajʿī* divorce).

Since the point of comparison is prohibition, and prohibition has two grades, a higher one characterized by permanence and respect, and a lower one devoid of both of these attributes, and since the implied sense of the predicate for the subject was: "they are wrong in that, because it is a lie," for the comparison, if its particle is dropped, cannot be taken literally so as to belong to the higher grade, even at its lowest level, that it is an irrevocable divorce, as they used to believe. And if the particle is retained, so as to belong to the lower grade, it is not valid, because it is forbidden, since legislation belongs only to God, and God did not legislate this. The explanation of both parts of the comparison conveys the meaning of the predicate with added explanation, so He omitted the predicate and sufficed with the explanation. He said, giving the reason for it, disparaging the *ẓihār* that the Arabs had become accustomed to, without anyone among the nations sharing in it: ﴿They are not their mothers⁠﴾, meaning: their wives are not their mothers, on the assumption that one of them intends the higher of the two grades of prohibition. The summary is that since they believed it to be an irrevocable divorce, they made themselves believe that the woman was a mother, because permanent prohibition is among the distinctive features of a mother. So they were addressed with this as a rebuke to them, because it is more effective as a deterrent. In Surat al-Aḥzāb there is what clarifies this.

Since they had been accustomed to this ruling in the *Jāhiliyyah*, and it had settled in their souls with a firmness that would not depart except through the utmost emphasis, He presented the speech in this manner in both parts, and said: ﴿Not⁠﴾, meaning: what ﴿their mothers⁠﴾ [are], in reality, ﴿except those who gave birth to them⁠﴾. Their wives did not give birth to them, so they are not forbidden to them with the permanent prohibition of honor and respect, nor are they among those who are attached to mothers in any valid way, such as the wives of the Prophet ﷺ, for they are mothers because of the right of honor, respect and reverence that they have, which no others have, since the Prophet ﷺ is greater in the fatherhood of religion than the biological father. Likewise the wet-nurses, because of their nursing, which is the function of a mother by origin. As for the wife, she is entirely different from all of that.

When He had finished explaining the first part in the most complete manner, He followed it with the explanation of the other part in the same way, and He said, linking it to the previous statement and emphasizing it, because they had become accustomed to saying it, so it had soaked into their hearts: ﴿And indeed they⁠﴾, meaning the ones who make *ẓihār*, ﴿say⁠﴾, meaning in this *ẓihār*, in every case, ﴿an objectionable word⁠﴾, which reality and the rulings deny. Ibn al-Mulaqqin said in *ʿUmdat al-Muḥtāj*: it is forbidden by consensus, as al-Rāfiʿī mentioned in the chapter on testimonies.

﴿And falsehood⁠﴾, meaning a statement deviating from correctness, departing from the intended aim, because the wife is prepared for enjoyment, which is in its ultimate end a form of humiliation, whereas the mother is at the furthest remove from that, because she is worthy of all respect. So she is neither a mother in reality, nor a likeness to one by a matter that the Lawgiver established for respect, such as nursing, or her being a bed for a great person such as the Prophet ﷺ or for a father, or for prohibition as in *liʿān* (mutual oath of condemnation). It is thus known that this statement is not true, nor does anything justify it. So it is pure falsehood. A briefer way to put this: since their *ẓihār* comprises an act and a statement, and the act is the prohibition, which is the locus of the point of comparison, and the custom regarding the point of comparison is that one is content with the least that the name applies to, but they had opposed that and made it at the highest level, which is permanent prohibition, which necessarily means that the likeness is in every respect in prohibition, and that is without any basis from God, whose ruling no one else has, He obliged them that the likeness be in every respect absolutely, so that they would be making the wife either a reality and not a claim, as they made the two prohibitions alike, without difference, but rather more so, because the likeness occurred between the two aspects and not between the two prohibitions. Then He made them aware of their ignorance regarding it, saying: ﴿They are not⁠﴾, to its end. When He made them aware of their ignorance in the act, He made them aware of their ignorance in the statement, so He said: [and] that they, to its end.

Al-Nawawī said in *al-Rawḍah*: the companions (of al-Shāfiʿī) said: *ẓihār* is forbidden, and it has two rulings: one is the prohibition of intercourse until the expiation (*kaffārah*) is performed, and the second is that the expiation becomes obligatory by returning (to the wife). End of quote. Although this statement conveys prohibition, it also conveys that she is forbidden to him in a narrow manner, its entry is hardship and its exit is difficult, so that its difficulty may deter him from falling into it. Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Qazzāz said in his comprehensive *Dīwān*: a man made *ẓihār* (ẓāhara) toward his wife and made *ẓihār* from his wife, when he said: "You are to me like the back of my mother," or "like a woman forbidden to me by kinship." They specifically singled out the back in *ẓihār* because the back is the place of riding, and the woman is the rider's mount in marriage, so this was used as a metaphor for that. It is as if he said: "Your riding upon me for marriage is like the riding of my mother." *Ẓihār* in the *Jāhiliyyah* was a divorce. For this reason the meaning of His words ﴿then they return to what they said⁠﴾ [al-Mujādilah: 3] became unclear.

Ibn al-Athīr said in *al-Nihāyah*: a man made *ẓihār* (ẓāhara) from his wife, and *tazaharra* and *tazāhara*, when he said to her: "You are to me like the back of my mother," and it was a divorce in the *Jāhiliyyah*. It is also said that they meant: "You are to me like the belly of my mother," that is, like her intercourse, so they used the back as an allusion for the belly, by way of proximity. It is also said that coming to a woman with her back toward the sky was forbidden among them, and the people of Medina used to say: if you come to a woman with her face toward the ground, the child will be born squint-eyed. So, by the intent of the absolute man among them to exaggerate the prohibition of his wife upon himself, he likened her to the back, then was not content with that, until he made her like the back of his mother. The verb *ẓihār* is followed by *min* (مِن), because when they made *ẓihār* against a woman, they kept away from her as they keep away from a divorced woman, and they avoided her. So it is as if his saying "ẓāhara min imraʾatihi" meant: he distanced himself from her and avoided her, just as it is said "ālā min imraʾatihi" (he swore off his wife), because the sense of distancing was implied, so it took *min*. End of quote. He said: Ibn al-Mulaqqin said in *al-ʿUmdah*, the commentary on *al-Minhāj*: it was a divorce in the *Jāhiliyyah*, and it was reported from the author of *al-Ḥāwī* that among them there was no revocation (*rajʿah*) in it. He said: so the Lawgiver transferred its ruling to prohibition after return and the obligation of expiation. End of quote. Abū Ḥayyān said: Abū Qilābah and others said: *ẓihār* in the *Jāhiliyyah* required among them a permanent separation.

Since the implied sense was: "Indeed God has forbidden it," He linked to it, encouraging repentance and calling to it, His statement, emphasizing it because of their belief in its severity and that there is no leniency in it: ﴿And indeed God⁠﴾, meaning the Greatest King, to whom no one has any command alongside Him in legislation or otherwise, ﴿is truly All-Pardoning⁠﴾, among His attributes is that He leaves punishment for whom He wills, ﴿All-Forgiving⁠﴾, among His attributes is that He erases the very trace of the sin and its effect, so that just as He does not punish for it, He does not reproach. So, is there anyone who repents, seeking pardon for his slip and the correction of what was amiss in him?

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 58, verse 3:

When He (glorified is He) denounced *zihar* (the pre-Islamic practice of a husband declaring his wife to be forbidden to him like his mother's back, *zihar*) and established its prohibition in the most emphatic and forceful manner, and since the customs that had prevailed would inevitably leave some remnants of it, He followed this with an explanation of the ruling on this occurrence and on what might happen of its like, saying: ﴿Those who divorce by zihar from their wives﴾. Since this was a statement of a ruling, He dropped the restriction (to Muslims) to make known that its generality includes the disbeliever just as it includes the Muslim, in order to convey the severity of the punishment for him, lest it be supposed that it applies only to the Arabs, whom He intended to denounce by stating that they alone practised it among all people. Therefore He said ﴿from their wives﴾ without saying "from among you."

Since the wording requires separation from the one to whom this was said, so that retaining her afterwards should be in the utmost remoteness, He, indicating this by the particle of distance, said ﴿then they go back﴾, that is, after this statement, ﴿on what they said﴾, either actually, by repeating this statement a second time, or potentially, by keeping her for a period of time in which this statement could be repeated a second time without separation by any expression of what God has linked separation to, such as divorce, release, or the like. Thus the one who makes zihar is considered to have returned to this statement in potentia, since it is possible for the statement to be repeated in that period. This is because custom dictates that whoever says a statement and does not conclusively settle it, carry it out, and enforce it, by returning to his statement a second time, and so on, has returned to it. Alternatively, the meaning may be: to annul what they said, so that they make lawful what they had made unlawful for themselves by not finalising a divorce. If the zihar was conditional, its ruling is not binding except upon the breaking of the condition. If he divorces immediately, well and good; otherwise the expiation (*kaffarah*) becomes binding upon him. The proper expression would be with *li-* (for), since it indicates continuity, as the situation requires, unlike *ila* (until), which indicates a delay and an interval. This applies to unrestricted zihar. As for zihar restricted to a day, a month, or the like, one does not return in it except by intercourse during the time in which the zihar was pronounced. Mere retention of her is not a return, because he retained her only for the lawfulness that he has in her after the time of the zihar.

Since the subject of the relative clause implies the meaning of a conditional, He placed the *fa'* (then) in its predicate to indicate causation, so that the obligation is repeated with the repetition of its cause, and so He said ﴿then the freeing of a neck﴾, that is, upon them, because of this zihar and return, is the freeing of ﴿a neck﴾, that is, one free of any defect that impairs work, fully a slave, and also restricted to ﴿a believing woman﴾, because this restriction was made in the expiation for killing, so this is to be interpreted in light of that. Also, because Mu'awiya ibn al-Hakam (may Allah be pleased with him) had a slave-girl, and he said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "I am under obligation to free a slave; shall I free her?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asked her about Allah, and she informed him of what indicated her monotheism. He said: "Who am I?" She said: "You are the Messenger of Allah." He said: "Free her, for she is a believer." Narrated by Malik and Muslim. Thus he justified the validity (of the manumission) by her faith, and did not ask him about the cause of the obligation. This shows that there is no difference between one obligation and another, and what makes the expiation obligatory is both the zihar and the return together, just as what makes the expiation obligatory in an oath is both the oath and the breaking of it together.

Since the freeing does not extend over the whole period before intercourse but occurs within part of it, He introduced the preposition and said ﴿before they touch one another﴾. Since what is intended is touching after the zihar and not touching in general, He said ﴿before they touch one another﴾, that is, a touching occurs between them anew, namely intercourse, whether the initiation of the contact is from him or from her, as indicated by the form of the reciprocal verb. This is forbidden before the expiation, even if it is the least and slightest form of touching, and even if it is indicated by the assimilation (of the letters), even if it is merely the penetration of the glans alone, with or without ejaculation. As for the preliminaries of intercourse, they are like those of a menstruating woman: they are not forbidden according to the more correct opinion. If he has intercourse, he has sinned, but no second expiation becomes obligatory, based on what al-Tirmidhi narrated from Salama ibn Sakhr (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about a man who makes zihar and has intercourse before expiating, and he said: "One expiation."

Since admonition is restraint from the act for which one is admonished, He began a new statement and said: ﴿That﴾, that is, this great, extremely severe restraint which applies to all of you without any doubt, ﴿you are admonished with it﴾, that is, it is a hardship that restrains you from returning to approaching such an act, let alone committing it, because whoever has made her unlawful to himself by Allah's prohibition, in his own claim, permanently, is as if he had killed her. And because that was with an expression he invented, by which he violated the sanctity of his mother, he was as if he had committed a sin by which he destroyed his whole self with a destruction that led him to kill her limb by limb, by freeing a neck equal to his own neck and to the neck of the one he had killed.

Since the implied sense is: "Allah is aware of what deters you," He followed this with His statement: ﴿And Allah﴾, that is, the One who has encompassing perfection. He placed the prepositional phrase first to indicate emphasis, to draw attention to the importance of compelling cessation from this, and so He said ﴿is aware of what you do﴾, that is, what you renew of its doing. ﴿Well-acquainted﴾, that is, knowing its outward and inward aspects, so He knows what expiates it. So do what Allah has commanded and stop at His limits.

Al-Qushayri said: [Zihar], although in reality it has no basis, nor any speech that confirms it, nor any law for it, after its matter was brought to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he hinted at something and said that it was his ruling, Allah did not leave it without an explanation by which He guided His law, so He judged in it with what the answer comprised, removing her complaint.

When the expiation (*kaffarah*) was ordered in stages, and the one who makes *zihar* (the pre-Islamic declaration that one's wife is like one's mother) is as if he had killed himself by killing the one he compared to his mother, as has passed, he needed something to revive himself. So freeing a slave (*'itq*), which is like giving life, was prescribed for him. When he is unable to do that, something is prescribed that causes his self to die, and causing it to die is for him a means of reviving it. The two months were half the period in which the soul is breathed into, so fasting them is like half the killing of the self that he committed. Its reviving of the spirit and restoring of the intellect is like its causing death. So God, glorified is He, made this a substitute for the killing, which is like giving life, and said: ﴿So whoever does not find﴾, that is, the slave that was commanded, because he is poor. If he is wealthy but his wealth is absent, he is considered as one who finds one. ﴿Then fasting﴾, that is, it is incumbent on him to fast ﴿two months﴾. Since the purpose is to break the self, as has passed, and continuity is more forceful in this, and for this reason Ramadan is called the month of patience, He restricted it by saying ﴿consecutive﴾, that is, in the most complete manner of consecutiveness, as far as is possible, which is what the explicit wording indicates. So if he breaks the consecutiveness by anything at all, even by forgetting the intention, he must start over. Fainting does not break the consecutiveness, because it is not within one's capacity. Likewise, breaking the fast due to menstruation, postpartum bleeding, or insanity does not break it, unlike breaking it due to travel, illness, or fear for a nursing or pregnant woman. This is because menstruation is known, so it is an exception by the law. The others are conditions that obscure the intellect and remove legal responsibility. As for illness and the like, it involves deliberately breaking the fast while the intellect is present.

Since abstaining from intimacy may extend beyond two months, He introduced the preposition and said ﴿before﴾, and He made the verbal noun explicit to indicate that it applies to whatever comes after the *zihar*, so He said ﴿they touch one another﴾. If he has intercourse at night, he disobeys, but the consecutiveness is not broken. Since feeding a person a meal equal to half a day's sustenance is like causing oneself to die by fasting a full day, the Exalted said: ﴿So whoever is not able﴾, that is, is not capable of fasting with complete capability, as the explicit mention of the *ta'* indicates, due to old age, illness, or excessive sexual desire that fasting would inflame. ﴿Then feeding﴾, that is, it is incumbent on him to feed ﴿sixty needy persons﴾, giving each needy person what sustains him for half a day. This is one *mudd* by the *mudd* of the Prophet ﷺ, which is about half a *qadah* by the Egyptian measure, equal to two handfuls cupped by the hands of a person of average build, of the staple food of the region. This is the same as in the *fitrah* (charity at the end of Ramadan). He omitted the condition of touching because it was mentioned in the first two (expiations). Perhaps the wisdom in specifying this one with it is that mentioning it at the start of the expiations is necessary, while repeating it in the second is because of the long duration of the fast, so abstaining from it during that period is a hardship. This (feeding) can be done in a brief moment, where there is no hardship in abstaining from touching during it. This applies if he returns (to the wife). If he joins the *zihar* with divorce, or one of them dies immediately before it is possible to divorce, then there is no expiation. Al-Baghawi said: this is because returning in speech is opposition. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, explained returning as regret, and said: they regret and return to harmony. This indicates what al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: if one makes *zihar* against a revocably divorced wife, his *zihar* takes effect. If he then takes her back, the expiation becomes obligatory on him, because taking back is a return.

When He mentioned the ruling, He explained its reason to encourage it, saying: ﴿That﴾, that is, this great concession to you, this kindness to you, and this healing clarification from the command of Allah, which conforms to the easy *hanifiyyah* (pure monotheistic faith), the religion of your father Ibrahim, upon whom be blessings and peace, is ﴿so that you may believe﴾, [that is], and this great, difficult act is so that your faith may be renewed and its reality established ﴿in Allah﴾, that is, the King to whom no one has any command, so that you obey Him by abandoning the practices of the Jahiliyyah ﴿and His Messenger﴾, whose veneration is part of venerating Him. He was sent with the religion of [his father] Ibrahim, upon both of them be blessings and peace. So if this severe ruling were abandoned in favor of what was practiced in the Jahiliyyah, it would be casting doubt on the mission with that easy religion.

When He encouraged this ruling, He warned against being lax about it, saying: ﴿And these﴾, that is, these purifying acts and whatever similar things preceded in this greatest Book, ﴿are the limits of Allah﴾, that is, the commands, prohibitions, and rulings of the greatest King, which must be obeyed, and adhered to in order to be observed with its full observance. So adhere to them, stop at them, and do not transgress them, for His retribution cannot be endured if His annulment or confirmation is violated. Since the implicit meaning was: "For those who believe in them are the gardens of bliss," He followed it with His saying ﴿And for the disbelievers﴾, that is, those who persist in disbelief [in them] or in any part of His laws, ﴿is a painful punishment﴾, because of the pain they inflicted on the believers through transgression.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 58, verse 5:

When He had mentioned His limits, and had hinted, by way of conjunction without a conjunctive antecedent, at the good tidings for its guardian, and had explicitly threatened those who transgress them, He followed this with a detailed account of their punishment, of which the good tidings to the believers of victory over them are a part. He said, emphasizing it because of their denial that they could be overcome despite their numbers and strength and the weakness and paucity of His party: ﴿Indeed, those who oppose Allah﴾, that is, who contend against the Sovereign Above concerning His limits, so as to make limits other than them. This is the form of enmity, renewing it and persisting in it by any kind of opposition [whatsoever] and even if it is hidden, by what the idghām (assimilation) points to, such as the opposition of the people of ittihad (unity of existence) who follow the ambiguous (mutashabih) and take it according to its apparent meaning, thereby corrupting the clear (muhkam) so that the whole Shari'ah is disrupted. For much of this surah was revealed concerning the hypocrites, the Jews and those who make truces, as will come in the discussion of secret counsel (al-najwa) and elsewhere. ﴿And His Messenger﴾, whose might is from His might. ﴿Will be humiliated﴾, that is, they will be thrown down, overturned on their faces, broken, debased and disgraced, so that they will not prevail, and will be turned back in their rage in [every] matter they aim at, from whatever humiliator it may be, in the easiest and least of matters. He expressed it in the past tense to indicate the certainty of its occurrence and the completion of its decree, as if it had already passed; therefore He said, so that the claim would be joined with its proof: ﴿As those before them were humiliated﴾. And since those who oppose [Allah and His Messenger] did not encompass all past times and places, He introduced the preposition, saying: ﴿before them﴾, that is, the opposers, such as the people of Noah and those after them who persisted in disobedience and did not yield to any proof or demonstration. Al-Qushayri said: Whoever neglects a Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and innovates a bid'ah (innovation) in his religion has entered this line and fallen into this humiliation.

When the discourse had fully attained its share of exposition, encouragement and warning, He turned to the beginning of the surah, or to what may be presumed, such as: "So there has been for you in what has passed, from the beginning of Islam until this time, what indicates that He, glorified is He, with victory and support, is with His Prophet ﷺ and his followers, may Allah be pleased with them, a lesson," [saying]: ﴿And We have certainly sent down﴾ [that is] with what We have of greatness upon you and upon those before you ﴿clear signs﴾, that is, great proofs which are in the utmost clarity regarding that and regarding everything upon which faith depends, by abandoning opposition, and through which submission is achieved. And since the implied sense was: "So for those who believe in them there is an enduring bliss in a secure station," He followed it with His saying: ﴿And for the disbelievers﴾ [that is] those firmly rooted in disbelief in them and in other commands of Allah, ﴿is a humiliating punishment﴾, because they were arrogant and deceived against the friends of Allah and His laws; that punishment will humiliate them, remove their might and their pride, and by it they will abandon their opposition.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 58, verse 6:

When he mentioned their punishment, he mentioned its time in a manner that confirms what had preceded regarding the comprehensiveness of His knowledge and the perfection of His power. So He said: ﴿On the Day when Allah raises them all up﴾, meaning: this will occur at the time when the Greatest King restores to life the disbelievers who were named and the believers who were alluded to, as they were, ﴿all together﴾ in a state of being gathered for the Resurrection. Since there is no greater pain than being rebuked in the presence of some people, how much more so when it takes place in the presence of all of them, and how much more so when it is before all of creation, both in sight and in hearing, He connected to this and followed His words with: ﴿then He will inform them﴾ [meaning] He will tell them with a great and exhaustive account ﴿of what they did﴾, as a disgrace for them and as the establishment of proof against them.

Since keeping account of all of this is a great matter, He resumed His words as an explanation of its ease for Him: ﴿Allah has enumerated it﴾, meaning He has encompassed it in number, quantity, quality, time and place, with all of the attributes of majesty and beauty that belong to Him. Since He mentioned His enumerating it, and it might have been thought that such enumeration is ordinarily possible, He negated that with His words: ﴿and they have forgotten it﴾, meaning all of them together, because it exceeds the limit of multiplicity, so how much more so each one individually. They forgot the sins they committed, out of carelessness about them, and that is itself carelessness toward Allah and audacity against Him. (p-358) Al-Qushayri said: When someone is called to account on the Day of Resurrection for a deed he did, what he did is presented to him, and then he remembers it until it is as though he has just risen from the carpet of his slip. The shame and regret that fall upon him are such that they make him forget every punishment in comparison. So the way of the Muslim is not to oppose the command of his Master, nor to hover around opposing His command. If what was decreed occurs and he falls into the disgrace of falling short, let him keep his slip in mind, and let him humbly supplicate Allah with a good entreaty.

Since the implied sense, indicated by the conjunction linking to something not mentioned, is: "So Allah is All-Knowing of everything of that and other than it," He connected to it His words: ﴿And Allah﴾, meaning with His all-encompassing power and comprehensive knowledge, ﴿is over all things﴾, absolutely, without any restriction whatsoever, ﴿Witness﴾, meaning Preserver, ever-present and not absent, and Watchful and not heedless. His preservation of it, His watching over it and His presence with it are exalted over it and overpowering it, by the encompassing of His dominion over everything, so that its preservation is possible in the most perfect manner He wills.

Abu Ja'far Ibn al-Zubayr said: When He, glorified is He, declared Himself free from the fabrications of the heretics, and made known that the entire world declares Him free from that through the tongues of its states, since the worlds bear witness against themselves by their need for a Wise One who brought them into existence, it is not possible for it to resemble anything of them. Rather He is exalted above their attributes and sanctified above their marks. So He said (p-359) ﴿Whatever is in the heavens and the earth glorifies Allah﴾ [al-Hadid: 1], and it passed, meaning He made Himself known by the greatness of His authority and the loftiness of His dominion. Then the address turned to His servants in His words ﴿Believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Hadid: 7], and so on to the verses after that. This was a kind of iltifat (a shift in the mode of address, from third person to second person). What occurs here is more akin to His words, glorified is He, in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30]. For after detailing the state of the righteous, the state of those placed at one of the extremes among them, and the state of those who resemble the righteous outwardly while being counted among the worst of disbelievers, when this pattern was complete He turned after it to calling the creation to worship Allah and to His Oneness: ﴿O people, worship your Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 21]. Then He turned the speech entirely and directed the address to making His Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, known before the creation: ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels: Indeed I am placing a successor on earth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30]. So this came as a kind of iltifat. Likewise, what occurs here: He, glorified is He, explained the state of the polytheists of the Arabs, condemned their obstinacy, reproached and rebuked them in a number of surahs, most of whose verses proceed in this manner and renew it, the first of them being Surat Sad, as He drew attention to in Surat al-Qamar, and up to the end toward which they were directed, until Surat al-Qamar came announcing the cutting off of their roots, and the warning that was alluded to was concluded in it. Likewise in Surat al-Rahman after it. Then He followed that with describing the state of the Hereafter's abode in Surat al-Waqi'ah, with added reproach and rebuke for their offenses, which called for glorifying Him, exalted is He, and sanctifying Him above their monstrous fabrications. So it was followed by Surat al-Hadid. Then in it He turned the address (p-360) to the believers, and this continued to the end of the surah. Surat al-Mujadilah proceeded on this same purpose, its address directed to an incident in which the believers were eager to learn its ruling, which was the zihar (a pre-Islamic form of divorce in which a husband likened his wife to his mother), whose matter is explained in it. So after His words ﴿Believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Hadid: 7], the speech does not go beyond touching upon the explanation of a ruling that befalls them. Then, the surahs that come after it up to the end of the Book mostly continued on this aim, since the purpose of making known the reports of the past generations and the earlier nations had been concluded, along with the rebuke and reproach of those who opposed, the mention of the example of the creation and their settlement in the Hereafter, and the mention of the details of the obligations and the recompense for them of reward and punishment, and what makes straight those who respond and believe, and what they must uphold according to the degrees and emphasis of obligations. When that was completed, the speech turned to what pertains to the believers in their rulings and to making known what is in it for their salvation. So most of the verses of any surah after this have this character, and if another matter enters, it is for a compelling need, which is the less frequent case, as we have explained. End.

(p. 361) Since this report of the comprehensiveness of His knowledge and the all-encompassing scope of His power, although it is self-evident to conceive, requires for those whom desire has led toward associationism (shirk), which entails deficiency, a proof [accompanying it], the Arabs used to deny that one God could encompass all people. Allah the Exalted said, indicating this with an empirical proof so that a person may benefit from what he sees of perceptible things, restricting the address to the highest of creation, as an indication that no one else can grasp this in its true sense: ﴿Do you not see﴾, meaning, you know with a knowledge that is in its clarity like seeing with the eye, ﴿that Allah﴾, meaning He who possesses all the attributes of perfection, ﴿knows what is in the heavens﴾, all of it.

Since the address is to the highest of creation, and the context concerns the comprehensiveness of knowledge, and since his addressing (ﷺ) with this was an indication to the listeners of the difficulty of this station, that it is such that scarcely anyone can conceive it or grasp it in its true sense except him (ﷺ) and those joined to him whose understanding is clear, whose mind is sound, and who are freed from desire and obstacles, [Allah] gathered and emphasized by repeating the relative pronoun. His singling him (ﷺ) out for the address, after it had been [addressed] to the manifest [polytheists] and then to the opponents, is an indication of honoring him, and its emphasis is a warning of the difficulty of the station, by generalization, so that it may be observed with due observance, fulfilling the right of instruction, just as the truthful one, the Mother of the Believers ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, observed it in her saying: "Glory be to Him whose hearing encompasses all voices," meaning His hearing of the woman's disputing, while it was in the utmost obscurity. Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿and what is on the earth﴾, meaning all of that in its universals and particulars, nothing of it is hidden from Him. The proof is that His management encompasses that in the most perfect manner, and He informs whomever He wills of His prophets and chosen servants of whatever He wills of the reports of that, the distant and the near, the present and the absent, the past (p. 362) and the future, and it occurs just as He informed.

Since that, although known, makes it impossible for a person to encompass every particular of it, He indicated it by what is closer to it. He said: ﴿there is no secret conversation﴾, with the feminine form (taknū, "there is not") in the reading of Abū Jaʿfar, because "najwā" (secret conversation) is feminine, as an indication of knowledge of it, even if it were weak to the utmost degree. The rest read it with the masculine form (yakūnu) because of the intervening element, and because the feminine is not real. In any case, it is from "kāna" (to be) in its complete usage. He generalized the negation with His saying: ﴿of any secret conversation﴾, meaning conversing parties, "najwā" was made to designate the conversers as an intensification. "Najwā" means secret speech and those who converse privately; it is both a noun and a verbal noun, as stated in the al-Qamus (the lexicon). ʿAbd al-Ḥaqq said in al-Wāʿī: "Najwā is speech between two persons, like a secret and consultation," end of quote. Its root is from "najwā," meaning the elevated part of the ground, and "najw" means extraction, cutting, skinning, excretion, and uncovering, because the one who speaks privately raises what is in his heart to his companion, extracts it by his private speech to him, cuts it from his heart, strips it from him, informs him, and reveals it.

Since secret conversation is not complete except with a third who preserves companionship by continuing the gathering, because two people become separated when one of them has a need, and they are like disputants in their private conferring and consulting, while the third is an intermediary between them, and since He, glorified be He, is (p. 363) odd and loves the odd, and three is the first of the odd numbers, just as He was preserving them in the beginning of beginnings, He said: ﴿three﴾, meaning in some state of affairs, ﴿but He is their fourth﴾, meaning He makes them four. So it is an active participle, and the meaning is by His knowledge and power, just as each of the conversers is aware of the secret speech of the others. Thus the essence of secret conversation is knowledge of the secret.

Since the three may have one of them wanting to be alone with another of them, so that the third remains alone, when they are four, companionship continues among them, but it is not complete except with a fifth who preserves the gathering if one of the two has a need. He said: ﴿nor five﴾, meaning of their secret speech, ﴿but He is their sixth﴾, similarly. The conclusion is that whenever there is an odd number, He, glorified be He, is its even partner, and as for His own oddness, it existed with nothing whatsoever alongside it at all, and it will be with no living thing alongside it. There is therefore no oddness in existence in the true sense except His.

Since it is known by repetition that what was mentioned is by way of example, not for a meaning specific to it, in terms of knowledge, He generalized with His saying: ﴿nor less than that﴾, beginning with the few because it comes before the many and is more hidden, ﴿than that﴾, meaning what was mentioned, namely the one, the two, and the four, which is far from its rank, even though He has honored it by absolutely affirming His companionship after it had no relation to them.

Since knowledge of the many is more difficult because of its dispersal, He said: (p. 364) ﴿nor more﴾, meaning of secret speech, ﴿than that﴾, such as six and what exceeds it without limit. This is the estimation according to the reading of the majority with a genitive, with a fatḥah on the rāʾ, while Yaʿqūb put it in the nominative, in the position of "min" in ﴿secret conversation﴾: ﴿but He is with them﴾, meaning He knows what passes among them and between them. From the comprehensiveness of His knowledge follows the comprehensiveness of His power, as was mentioned in Ṭā-Hā, so that His witnessing may be complete.

Since generality in place entails generality in time, and place is more evident to the senses, He said: ﴿wherever﴾, meaning in whatever place, ﴿they may be﴾. For there is no distance between Him and anything, since He is the One who created distance, and His knowledge of things is not due to nearness of place, so that it would vary with differing places, nor by any cause other than His existence as He is with the attributes of perfection. Al-Rāzī said: "The Truth has neither separated from created beings nor joined them. How could He separate from them when He is their originator, their preserver, and their manifester? And how could eternity join with the temporal when by Him all things subsist, and He is the Self-Subsisting over all?" end of quote. The conclusion is that nothing in the world is hidden from Him, glorified be He, even if it reaches such fineness as to be indivisible. He witnesses all of that in preservation, knowledge, comprehensiveness, and presence. The sign of this in His creation is that the whole body is quickened by the spirit, so no part of it remains except that it is preserved by the spirit (p. 365), by which it perceives. He, glorified be He, is not veiled from His knowledge, nor is any of His attributes veiled. Thus the companionship is established, while He is such that place does not contain Him and number does not limit Him. He holds created things and expands them. Created beings, their attributes, their acts, and any meaning of theirs do not ascend to any of His attributes. For Him there is from place the position of exaltation, from knowledge the highest degree, and from the names and attributes what they require. Ibn Burjān alluded to this and said: "Whoever reflects on what he has read and understands what he has learned will attain of verification what we are in the way of explaining, as much as has been decreed for him. Do you not see that the jinn, where is their place, even though they are described as having a place? Then the angels are higher in rank and station. Indeed, the spirit, of the whole body that carries it, by it it is quickened, by it its management is carried out, and by it it stands, by the permission of Allah, its Creator."

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said in his greatest sermon, which was the last sermon he delivered, related by al-Ḥārith ibn Abī Usāmah: He mounted the pulpit and said: "O people, come close and make room for those behind you," three times. The people drew near and pressed together, and they turned and saw no one. A man among them said after the third time: "For whom should we make room, O Messenger of Allah, for the angels?" He said: "No, for when they are with you, they are not before you [nor behind you], but on your right and on your left." [And according to that] they are not in the place of the right (p. 366) and left here, but in the place beyond that. So Allah, majestic is His majesty, is higher, more exalted, purer in station, and more noble in being established, end of quote.

Since man is forgetful, especially if time has prolonged its course over him, He said, conjoining to what its implication is: He keeps account of their movements and stillnesses, their words, their deeds, and their conditions, and preserves them throughout the length of time, just as He was preserving them before their creation, and before the beginning of beginnings. ﴿Then He will inform them﴾, meaning He will tell their possessors with a great informing, ﴿of what they did﴾, both minute and great, ﴿on the Day of Resurrection﴾, which is the greatest purpose of existence, for the manifestation of the Exalted Attributes therein in the most complete manifestation.

When the Exalted informed of this great matter, He gave as its reason what is evidence of witnessing, and He said, emphasizing for what they had of denial, whether by word or deed, through the association that entails deficiency: ﴿Indeed, Allah﴾, meaning He to whom all perfection belongs. Since the station calls for emphasis on the comprehensiveness of knowledge, He placed the prepositional phrase first, as the indication to it has passed more than once. He said: ﴿of all things﴾, of what was mentioned and other than it, ﴿is Knowing﴾, meaning of utmost knowledge. So He is powerful over all things, and He is a witness over all things, because the relation of His most holy essence to all things is equal, with no difference whatsoever between one thing and another. Al-Qushayrī said: "The companionship of the Truth, glorified be He, though it is general in knowledge and sight and specific in favor and support, has a great effect on the hearts of the people of gnosis in this address, until the matter ends with them in (p. 367) interpretation. So for the bewildered and the amazed, in the veil of hearing this, there is a delightful spring."

[p. 368] Since this proof is also one whose full grasp is difficult, He (exalted is He) pointed to it through a particular event that actually occurred, one whose reality is known to the one spoken to. If he persists in obstinacy after that, then words will fail him except through the edge of the sword. ﴿Have you not seen﴾, that is, do you not know with a knowledge that is like sight? He indicated the lowliness of the rank of those seen by distancing them from the highest of people in status, using the particle of limit (ilā, "to"), and so said: ﴿to those who﴾. Since the intelligent person is one who, when restrained from something, refrains from it until it becomes clear to him that there is no harm upon him in doing what he was restrained from, He used the passive form and said: ﴿were forbidden﴾, that is, by one who forbids, that which the one forbidden should not oppose until he knows that he is safe from harm, ﴿from secret conferring﴾, that is, secret speech, because by it they expose themselves to the place of suspicion, in a way that is not pleasing to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). As Abu al-'Ala' al-Ma'arri said:

"A friend is like water: it reveals to me his inner thoughts with clarity, and hides them from turbidity."

Since the one who forbids is Allah, and this is worthy of being kept as far as possible from Him, He used the particle of delay and said: ﴿then they return﴾, that is, in a manner of persistence, because if it occurred once they would hasten to repent of it, or it would be a lapse pardoned. ﴿to what they were forbidden﴾, that is, without preparing for the harm that may be expected from the one who forbids, [p. 368 continues] ﴿and they confer﴾, that is, all of them turn to secret conferring with a single turn, so that each of them does what the other does, time after time, in a manner of persistence. The reading of Hamzah, "wa-yantijūna" (in the form of ifti'āl), indicates deliberateness and obstinacy. ﴿in sin﴾, that is, in that by which sin is written against them, through wrongdoing, lying, and what is not lawful. Since He mentioned the general, He followed it with the restricted by its severity, and said: ﴿and enmity﴾, that is, the enemy, which is the extreme of intending evil by excessive transgression of limits. Since this is evil in itself, He followed it with an indication that a thing's description changes in relation to the one toward whom it is done, so it grows greater with the greatness of the one disobeyed, and so He said: ﴿and disobedience to the Messenger﴾, that is, the one who came to them from the Supreme King, and he is complete in messengership, being sent to all creation and in every age, so there is no prophet after him; therefore he deserves the utmost honor.

Since He brought the magnification of the sin to its limit, He signaled wrath by turning the speech to address, and so said: ﴿And when they come to you﴾, O Messenger, the greatest, to whom revelation comes from the One who sent him, and who is never absent from him at all, because He is All-Encompassing in knowledge and power, ﴿they greet you﴾, that is, they confront you with what they prepare as a greeting, from their saying: "as-sāmm ʿalayka" (death be upon you) and the like. He generalized every expression by His saying: ﴿with what Allah has not greeted you with﴾, that is, the Supreme King, with whom there is no command for anyone. Whoever goes beyond what He has legislated has exposed himself to His wrath. Among what enters this is the saying of some people to others, "ṣabāḥ al-khayr" (good morning) and the like, turning away from the greeting of peace. Since it was well known of them that they hid this with all their effort and made it public, relying on Allah's granting them respite that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would not perceive it, and if he perceived it he would not be able to take vengeance upon them, He expressed this by His saying: ﴿and they say﴾, that is, at the time of being led on by respite, renewing their saying and persisting in it, ﴿within themselves﴾, without informing anyone of it: ﴿Why does Allah not punish us﴾, that is, why not, and why does He not, Him to whom belongs all-encompassing knowledge of everything according to the claim of those who deceive us, ﴿for what we say﴾, renewing it with persistence, if He dislikes it, as Muhammad (ﷺ) says.

Since this contained His knowledge (glorified and exalted is He) of this particular matter concerning these people, it is established by it that His knowledge encompasses everything in existence, because the relation of all things to Him is on one equal footing. So when His knowledge of a part is established, His knowledge of the whole is established, [and thus His power over the whole is established], and so He is over everything a witness. He said, threatening them and indicating that it is not appropriate for anyone to say such a thing unless he is certain that no punishment will befall him, or that what befalls him from it is something he does not care about, and then He repelled them with His strength: ﴿Sufficient for them is﴾, that is, their recompense in vengeance against them and in their punishment, and in being pelted with the arrows of its flame, the piercing of its sparks, and the striking of its thunderbolts: ﴿Jahannam﴾, that is, the layer that meets them with scowling, frowning, aversion, and harshness. If they receive punishment in this world, it would be [p. 370] an addition beyond what suffices; so their seeking punishment hastily is pure foolishness. ﴿they will burn in it﴾, that is, they will suffer its punishment continually, for I have prepared it for them. Since the implied meaning is that they will surely come to it, His saying was caused by this: ﴿and wretched is the destination﴾, that is, their destination. The cause of this was that the Jews and the hypocrites used to confer among themselves, looking at the believers and winking, deceiving them into thinking they were conferring about what would distress them. The believers would then suppose that some news had reached them of their brothers who had gone out in expeditions as warriors in the way of Allah, of killing or defeat, and so this would grieve them. They complained of this to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he forbade them from conferring in this situation, but they did not desist. Ahmad, al-Bazzar, and al-Tabarani narrated with a chain of transmission (the commentator al-Haythami said in al-Majma' that it is sound, because Hammad heard from ʿAṭāʾ ibn al-Sāʾib during his sound state of mind) from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr (may Allah be pleased with him and his father): "The Jews used to say to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): 'As-sām ʿalayka (death be upon you).' Then they would say within themselves: ﴿Why does Allah not punish us for what we say?﴾ So this was revealed." Abu Ya'la narrated from Anas (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Prophet (ﷺ) said at that time: "If any of the People of the Book greets you with peace, say: 'wa-ʿalayka' (and upon you)."

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 58, verse 9:

When He had forbidden secret consultation (najwa), and censured those who engage in it, and threatened for it, this was a place where one might suppose that the prohibition is general for every secret consultation, even if it is for good. So He resumed His speech, calling out with the particle after which what follows carries no great weight, and addressing them by the first of the teeth of faith (awwal asnan al-iman), as the situation requires for it: ﴿O you who have believed﴾, that is, who claim that they have brought this reality into being; ﴿when you consult privately﴾, that is, each of you lifts speech from himself, raising it and disclosing it secretly to his companion; ﴿then do not consult privately﴾, that is, do not bring this reality into being openly, like the consultation of the hypocrites; ﴿in sin﴾, that is, wrongdoing, and every act for which punishment is written on account of it; ﴿and transgression﴾, that is, the one which is severe enmity by means of what harms, even if the transgressor thinks that no sin is recorded against him for it.

When the prohibition was general, He particularized, saying: ﴿and disobedience to the Messenger﴾. Since the context is to honour the Prophet ﷺ, although the reality of sin is known only from him, He said, exalted is He: ﴿and disobedience to the Messenger﴾, that is, the one perfect in messengerhood, for such disobedience disturbs his thought, so that he does not leave him to convey the messages of his Lord while his chest is expanded and his soul is content.

When it was known that their prohibition concerns only evil that corrupts the relations between them, which is what they do not want the Prophet ﷺ to be informed of, He stated explicitly, urging the reform of relations between people, because the best of affairs is that which returns with reform by it, and the worst of affairs is that which returns with corruption by it: ﴿but consult together in righteousness﴾, that is, in the wide good in which is the goodness of upbringing (husn al-tarbiyah). (p-372) Since that may be done by nature, He urged the righteous intention by His saying: ﴿and piety﴾, which is that what is in one's self is evidently a veil that protects from the punishment of God, by being pleasing to God and His Messenger.

Since piety is the mother of all good qualities, He emphasized it and drew attention to it by His saying: ﴿and fear God﴾, that is, intend with an intention that is followed by action, that you place between yourselves and the wrath of the Greatest King a shield. Since the remembrance of the Hereafter is the gathering place of all fears, especially the disgracing of secrets before the heads of witnesses, He said: ﴿to whom you will be gathered﴾, that is, specifically, ﴿you will be gathered﴾, that is, assembled with the easiest and most facile matter, by compulsion and against your will; and that is the Day of Resurrection, in which He, glorified is He, manifests Himself to judge among creatures and to do justice among them with fairness, and to call them to account for the speck and the fibre, nothing hidden from Him and no shield protecting from Him; in it the pavilions of greatness are unveiled, the full effect of the Word becomes manifest, the blows of domination are displayed in the arenas of might, and the flashes of pride are scattered. So if you do that, keeping this in mind, you will not undertake anything you wish to conceal from the Prophet ﷺ, and that will be more soothing to his eye and purer for you.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 58, verse 10:

When He (glory be to Him) had emphasized the matter of secret consultation (najwa), which only the people of hypocrisy would engage in, it might have occurred to someone that harm would come to the people of the religion from it. So He said, speaking privately to the sincere believers and frightening the hypocrites, and making clear that its harm returns only upon them: ﴿Secret counsel is only from Satan﴾, i.e., the well-known najwa, which is what is forbidden, namely, what its speaker dislikes to have the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) become aware of. It is said: it is what Satan imagines to a person of disliked rulings. ﴿From Satan﴾, i.e., originating from the one who was burned, by being expelled from the mercy of Allah the Exalted, for he is the one who drives people to it by making it appear attractive. So whoever performs it follows the greatest of his enemies, in opposition to His allies.

When He had made clear that it is from him, He explained what drives him to make it appear attractive, saying: ﴿so that he may grieve﴾, i.e., Satan, in order to cast grief into the hearts of ﴿those who believe﴾, i.e., he makes them imagine that because of something, something harmful has occurred to them. Al-huzn (grief) is a severe concern and an ache which softens the heart; ḥazanahu and aḥzanahu have the same meaning. In al-Qamus he says: "Or aḥzanahu: to make him sad, and ḥazanahu: to put grief into him." Accordingly, Nafi's reading "yuḥzina" (from aḥzana) is stronger in meaning than the reading of the majority.

Since this might suggest to one in whose heart is a sickness that Satan has some power over things [of the things], He removed that by His saying: ﴿but it will not harm them﴾, i.e., Satan and what he drove them to of secret conversation, and He emphasized the negation with the preposition (al-jarr), saying: ﴿in the least﴾, i.e., (p-374) those who believe, ﴿anything﴾ of harm, however little and however hidden, as conveyed by the doubling (idgham). ﴿Except by the permission of Allah﴾, i.e., by the enabling of the King who encompasses everything in knowledge and power. Al-Shaykhan narrated from Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both) that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When you are three, let not two speak privately apart from the third, except by his permission, for that grieves him."

Since the implied sense is: it is known that no one is to be feared but Allah, for nothing is carried out except what He wills, so the ones under His lordship should fear Him alone, He followed it with His saying: ﴿And upon Allah﴾, i.e., the King who has no equal, not upon anyone else, ﴿let the believers put their trust﴾, i.e., those firmly rooted in faith, in all their affairs, for He alone is able to set them right or corrupt them. And let them not grieve over anyone who plots against them, whether secretly or openly, for when they place their trust in Him and entrust their affairs to Him, He does not permit their grief, and if they do not, He lets them grieve. He specified "those firmly rooted" because this is possible for them in the ordinary course; as for the beginners (ahl al-bidayat), this does not occur from them except as a breaking of habit (kharq 'adah).

When he mentioned what grieves, namely secret conversation, which involves excluding the one sitting beside him from speech and so gives rise to suspicion of resentment and the distancing of hearts, he followed it with exclusivity in the assembly (majlis), which is the separation of bodies. This entails the same suspicion that secret speech entails, and from it arises grief. He thereby informed them of His complete mercy and perfect compassion by attending to (p-375) good manners among them, even though these belong to customary matters rather than the rulings of worship. He addressed the people of the lower rank of faith, because they are the ones who need this kind of manners, saying: ﴿O you who have believed﴾. He urged them to comply by this description. ﴿When it is said to you﴾, that is, by whatever speaker it may be, for good is desired for its own sake: ﴿make room﴾, that is, expand, that is, impose upon yourselves the widening of places ﴿in the assemblies﴾, that is, in sitting, or in their place, for the sake of one who comes and finds no seat in which to sit. By "assembly" is meant the genus of place in which they remain, whether sitting or standing, in prayer or otherwise, since it is fit for sitting. This applies in every age, and the assembly of the Prophet (ﷺ) is more deserving of this. The reading of ʿĀṣim (qirāʾah of ʿĀṣim) with the plural form clarifies that the genus is intended. ﴿Then make room﴾, that is, widen within it with breadth of heart. ﴿Allah will make room﴾, that is, He to whom belongs the whole matter and perfect greatness, ﴿for you﴾, in every matter whose narrowness you dislike, in both abodes.

Since widening may be achieved by shifting aside while continuing to sit, and at other times the need calls for standing in order to move from one place to another, he said: ﴿And when it is said﴾, that is, by a speaker, as previously mentioned, if he intends reform (p-376) and good: ﴿rise up﴾, that is, stand up and get up to the place to which you are ordered or to which the situation calls, for widening or for other commands such as prayer, jihad, and others. ﴿So rise up﴾, [that is] so stand up and get up. ﴿Allah will raise﴾, He to whom belong all attributes of perfection. He expressed Himself with the Majestic Name and repeated it explicitly in place of a pronoun, to encourage compliance, because the self is stingy with what opposes what is familiar. ﴿Those who have believed﴾, even if they are not scholars, ﴿among you﴾, O you who are commanded to make room, who listen to commands and hasten to them, in this world and the Hereafter, with victory and good remembrance, through firmly possessing the attribute of faith, which necessitates loftiness of rank, by their obedience to His Messenger (ﷺ), and by the breadth of their hearts in widening for their brothers.

Since the believer may not be among those known for knowledge, he said: ﴿And those who have been given knowledge﴾. Since knowledge in itself is sufficient for elevation without regard to a specific giver, he used the passive form ﴿have been given knowledge﴾, that is, while they are believers, ﴿degrees﴾: one degree by complying with the command, another by faith, and a degree by the excellence of their knowledge and precedence. Al-Ṭabarānī and Abū Nuʿaym, in Kitāb al-ʿIlm, related from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever death comes to while he is seeking knowledge in order to revive Islam, the Prophets will not exceed him except by one degree." It was related by al-Dārimī and Ibn al-Sunnī in Riyāḍat al-Mutaʿallimīn from al-Ḥasan, without attribution. Our shaykh said: it is said that he is al-Baṣrī, so it would be a mursal (report). And from al-Zubayr: knowledge is masculine, so only the males of men love it.

Whenever a person is more knowledgeable, he is more mindful. Perhaps he omitted the restriction "from" (min) in this phrase, even though it is intended, in order to convey that knowledge elevates its possessor absolutely. If he is a believer acting upon his knowledge, it is the utmost; if he is disobedient, he is higher than a disobedient believer who is devoid of knowledge; and if he is a disbeliever, his elevation is worldly in comparison with a disbeliever who has no knowledge. He indicated this by concluding the verse with His saying, encouraging and warning: ﴿And Allah﴾, that is, while the One encompassing everything in power and knowledge ﴿is Aware of what you do﴾, that is, the state of the command and other matters, ﴿Acquainted﴾, that is, knowing of its outward and inward.
